Formulation:  
A young woman with no prior migraine diagnosis experiencing new onset of unilateral left-sided throbbing headaches with typical migraine features including visual aura, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting. Occupational stress and recent personal losses accentuate health anxiety. Use of oral contraceptives and headache exacerbation with neck movement warrants consideration of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) as a differential, although no neurological deficits or systemic signs are present. Patient’s fear of brain tumor is heightened due to personal connections; no focal signs or progressive symptoms reduce likelihood of serious intracranial pathology presently. Psychosocial stressors may contribute to symptom perception and distress. Protective insight and cooperative attitude support favorable prognosis.  

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Migraine headache  
- Patient Goal(s): Understand and manage headache symptoms; reduce frequency and severity; alleviate anxiety about serious causes  
- Clinical Goal(s): Confirm diagnosis; initiate symptomatic treatment; reduce headache episodes; monitor for red flags; provide reassurance  
- Actions (Patient): Maintain headache diary noting triggers, severity, and associated symptoms; take prescribed analgesics/anti-inflammatories as advised; report worsening symptoms promptly  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Recommend symptomatic treatment with paracetamol, co-codamol, ibuprofen or naproxen; advise headache diary; educate patient about migraine and potential triggers; schedule follow-up in one week; counsel on red flag symptoms requiring urgent review  

Secondary Problem: Risk of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST)  
- Patient Goal(s): Gain clarity on cause of headache; avoid serious complications  
- Clinical Goal(s): Monitor for neurological signs; rule out CVST if symptoms worsen or persist; arrange appropriate imaging if indicated  
- Actions (Patient): Be alert for new neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness, vision changes); seek urgent care if symptoms develop or worsen  
- Actions (Clinician/GP): Provide safety netting advice; consider imaging if clinical condition changes; review risk factors including oral contraceptive use  

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes  
- Topics Covered: Nature of migraine headaches, common triggers, differentiation from serious causes (CVST, tumor, meningitis), importance of headache diary, medication use, signs needing urgent medical review  
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Increasing headache intensity, persistence beyond usual duration, new neurological deficits, worsening vision, neck stiffness, fever  
- Coping Strategies: Rest, use of analgesics as prescribed, avoid triggers once identified, stress management advised though not formally addressed  

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Implied (participated actively, agreed with plan)  
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded  
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: None reported  
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not applicable  
- Review Date: One week from initial consultation recommended  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Migraine - High likelihood: Classic presentation with unilateral throbbing headache, visual aura, photophobia, nausea, vomiting; no neurological deficits  
- Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis (CVST) - Medium likelihood: Oral contraceptive use plus neck movement worsening headache raise suspicion, but no focal deficits or systemic signs observed  
- Brain Tumor - Low to Medium likelihood: Patient concern due to symptoms and personal context, but no neurological signs or progression typical of tumor currently
